newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to study CNN request to open bureau in Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to study CNN request to open bureau in Cuba.

text.p: The United States will study a request for a license made by Cable News Network (CNN), a subsidiary of Time Warner Inc, to open a bureau in Cuba, a State Department spokesman said on Friday.
The department's chief spokesman, Nicholas Burns, said CNN had asked for the reactivation of a request submitted earlier this year for a license to establish an office in Havana.
"We're going to look at this very, very carefully and I think we will try to make the best decision that we can," Burns told reporters at a briefing.
The Cuban government announced on Thursday that it had authorized CNN to open what would become the first U.S. news bureau in Havana in three decades.

But under regulations stemming from Washington's economic embargo against Cuba, any U.S. news organization seeking to set up shop in the communist-ruled island must first obtain a license from the Treasury Department.
Burns said both the State and the Treasury departments, as well as the White House, would study the matter, taking into consideration the laws and rules governing links with Cuba.

The United States will also weigh factors such as the interest of other U.S. news organizations that want to open bureaux in Cuba and whether news generated by U.S. outfits would be available to the Cuban people.
"We need to look at this in light of all those regulations. It's a very important issue for us right now (and) we are giving it high-level attention," Burns added.
The United States has maintained economic and trade sanctions against Cuba since 1962 to try to isolate and weaken the government of President Fidel Castro.
In a bid to foster cultural contacts with the island, in October, 1995 President Bill Clinton said he would authorize U.S. news organizations to open reporting operations in Cuba.
Several companies expressed interest but the process was halted in February after Cuba shot down two U.S. civilian aircraft over the Florida straits, killing four Cuban exiles from Miami.

Shortly after that incident, Clinton signed into law the Helms-Burton Act, which tightened the embargo. One provision fixes rules for the opening of U.S. news bureaux in Cuba, among them that the exchange must be "fully reciprocal."

Nevertheless, a spokesman for one of the law's authors, North Carolina Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, said the veteran chairman of the Foreign Relations committee was not against the idea of CNN going to Cuba.
"In principle, we are not opposed to it, in fact, we like the idea of CNN and other legitimate news organizations doing more intensive reporting in Cuba," said committee spokesman Marc Thiessen.
"We'd have to see the fine print and find out what Castro is looking for and what he wants in exchange," he added.

Thiessen said the reciprocity rule in Helms-Burton was aimed at forcing Cuba to allow U.S. government-funded outfits like Radio Marti to open in Havana if Cuba wanted to establish bureaux for its own state-run media in the United States.
